analogy.p: Think of the sine rule as a set of matched pairs: every angle is paired with the side directly across from it, and the ratio side-to-sine is the same for every pair, like three identical gear ratios in one machine. Once you have one working pair you can drive the others. The cosine rule is like a hinge: two sides are the arms of a door, the angle between them is how far the door is open, and the third side is the gap between the door's tip and the frame. Open the hinge to exactly 90 degrees and you get Pythagoras; open it wider and the gap grows beyond Pythagoras, which is what the correction term does. The analogy breaks down because a real hinge cannot have an angle over 180 degrees and does not show why the ratio in the sine rule equals the circumcircle's diameter.
analogy.t: A seesaw of matching pairs and a hinge

bullets: **Sine rule**: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C (or the flipped version sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c when finding an angle).
**Cosine rule**: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, which can be rearranged to cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc) to find an angle.
**Area of a triangle**: Area = ½ab sin C, where C is the angle **between** sides a and b.
You must choose the correct rule from the information given, which is a skill examiners reward directly with a method mark.
These rules work for **any** triangle: acute, obtuse or right-angled.
Answers are normally required to 3 significant figures (lengths) or 1 decimal place (angles) unless the question says otherwise; keep full calculator accuracy until the final line.
They are used inside longer questions on bearings, 3D shapes, circle geometry, vectors and area of segments.
core.h: What the specification asks you to do
core.p: The Edexcel Higher specification says you must know and apply the **sine rule** and the **cosine rule** to find unknown lengths and angles in triangles that do **not** have a right angle, and use **area = ½ab sin C** to calculate the area of a triangle. These three formulae let you solve any triangle when you are given enough information, and they are heavily tested on Paper 2 and Paper 3 (calculator papers) as 3 to 6 mark problem-solving questions. They are not given on the formula sheet in every series, so you must memorise them. Everything in this topic is an extension of right-angled trigonometry (SOHCAHTOA), which only works when one angle is exactly 90 degrees.

bullets: The side opposite an angle is the side that does **not touch** that angle; it is the side the angle 'looks at'.
Side BC is called a, side AC is called b, and side AB is called c.
A good habit is to **redraw the triangle** large and label every side and angle with the given numbers before choosing a rule.
Mark the unknown with a letter such as x, and mark which letters of the formula you will use.
The three angles of any triangle add up to **180 degrees**, so if you know two angles you can always find the third; this is often the first step of a sine rule question.
In the cosine rule the angle used in cos must be the one **opposite** the side on the left of the equals sign.
If a question gives the triangle as 'ABC with AB = 8 cm' then c = 8, because AB is opposite C.
core.h: The labelling convention (get this right first)
core.p: In every formula the triangle is labelled ABC with **capital letters for angles at the vertices** and **lower-case letters for the sides**. The side with lower-case letter a is the side **opposite** angle A, b is opposite B, and c is opposite C. This convention is what makes the sine rule work, because the rule pairs every angle with the side directly across the triangle from it. If your triangle is labelled with other letters (for example PQR) you simply relabel in your head or rewrite the formula using the question's letters, such as p / sin P = q / sin Q.

bullets: **Sine rule** is used for AAS (two angles and any side), ASA (two angles and the side between them) and SSA (two sides and a non-included angle).
**Cosine rule** is used for SAS (two sides and the angle **between** them) and SSS (three sides).
The test: 'Do I have a side and its opposite angle both known?' If yes, the sine rule can start. If no, it is the cosine rule.
Right-angled triangle? Use Pythagoras or SOHCAHTOA instead; they are quicker and examiners expect them.
If you need an area and you know two sides and the angle between them, use **½ab sin C** directly.
If an area question gives the area and asks for an angle or side, rearrange ½ab sin C = area.
Some questions need **both** rules in one go, for example the cosine rule to find a missing side and then the sine rule to find an angle.
For a first step in a multi-step question, ask: which triangle contains the most known values?
core.p: Deciding which rule to use is the key exam skill. Look at what is **given** and what you are asked to **find**. If you know a side **and the angle opposite it** (a matching pair) and you are looking for another side or angle that is linked to one more known value, use the **sine rule**. If you do not have a matching pair, you must use the **cosine rule**. The cosine rule is needed in two situations: you know two sides and the **included** angle (SAS) and want the third side, or you know all three sides (SSS) and want an angle.

bullets: Use the form **a / sin A = b / sin B** when finding a **side** (the unknown is on the top, so you multiply to rearrange).
Use the flipped form **sin A / a = sin B / b** when finding an **angle** (the unknown is on the top, so only a single multiplication is needed before inverse sine).
The longest side is opposite the largest angle; the shortest side is opposite the smallest angle. Use this to check your answer is sensible.
If angle A is 90 degrees the sine rule gives a / 1 = b / sin B, so sin B = b / a, which is ordinary SOH in a right-angled triangle; the sine rule includes SOHCAHTOA as a special case.
The sine rule needs one **complete pair** (angle with its opposite side) plus one other piece of information.
Write the equation with the numbers substituted **before** rearranging, so you earn the method mark even if the arithmetic goes wrong.
The value a / sin A is also equal to the **diameter of the circumcircle** of the triangle (the circle through all three vertices), which links to circle geometry.
core.h: The sine rule: statement and why it works
core.p: The sine rule states that in any triangle, the ratio of a side to the sine of its opposite angle is the same for all three sides: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C. It works because if you drop a perpendicular height h from one vertex, then h = b sin C = c sin B, which gives b / sin B = c / sin C, and the same argument works for the other pairs. A larger angle always faces a longer side, and the sine rule is just the exact version of that fact. You only ever use **two** of the three fractions at a time.

bullets: Step 1: label the triangle and find any missing angle using angles in a triangle sum to 180.
Step 2: write a / sin A = b / sin B, choosing the pair that contains your unknown and your known matching pair.
Step 3: substitute the numbers, for example x / sin 65 = 7.2 / sin 48.
Step 4: multiply both sides by sin 65 to get x = 7.2 sin 65 / sin 48.
Step 5: calculate, then round to 3 significant figures and include the units.
Sense check: is the longest side opposite the biggest angle?
Never round the value of a sine to 2 or 3 d.p. during the working; use the calculator's full answer or the ANS key.
If the unknown is on the **bottom** of the fraction, flip both fractions first, or cross-multiply and then divide.
core.h: Using the sine rule to find a side
core.p: To find a side you need two angles and one side (so you can calculate the third angle if necessary). Write the sine rule with the unknown side on the **top-left**: x / sin(angle opposite x) = known side / sin(its opposite angle). Then multiply both sides by the sine to isolate x. Always check the calculator is in degree mode, because radian mode is the single most common source of wrong answers in this topic.

bullets: Step 1: write sin A / a = sin B / b with the unknown angle on top.
Step 2: substitute the numbers and rearrange: sin B = b sin A / a.
Step 3: apply sin⁻¹ to get B and round to 1 decimal place.
Check: if the side opposite the angle you are finding is the **longest side**, the angle could be obtuse, so think carefully.
An angle in a triangle can be found as 180 minus the calculator value if the diagram shows it is obtuse.
The sine of an angle and the sine of 180 minus that angle are equal, for example sin 30 = sin 150 = 0.5.
Once you know two angles, the third is 180 minus their sum, so you can then find the last side by the sine rule again.
If sin B comes out bigger than 1, the triangle is impossible; recheck your substitution.
core.h: Using the sine rule to find an angle
core.p: To find an angle, use the flipped version so that the unknown angle is on the top: sin A / a = sin B / b. Substitute, multiply both sides by the known side that sits under the unknown angle, and then use **inverse sine** (sin⁻¹) on your calculator. Because the inverse sine only returns an angle between 0 and 90 degrees, you should be alert to whether the angle in the triangle could be obtuse. In most GCSE questions the angle is obviously acute (for example when the opposite side is not the longest), but the situation is worth checking.

bullets: Example: A = 30 degrees, b = 10, a = 7 gives sin B = 10 sin 30 / 7 = 0.714..., so B = 45.6 degrees **or** B = 134.4 degrees.
Both are valid here because 30 + 134.4 = 164.4 which is less than 180, leaving 15.6 degrees for C.
If the side opposite the known angle is **longer** than the other known side, only the acute solution is possible.
If a is shorter than b but longer than b sin A, there are two triangles; if a equals b sin A there is exactly one (right-angled); if a is shorter than b sin A, no triangle exists.
In an exam, if the diagram shows an obtuse angle at B, use 180 minus your calculator value.
The cosine rule does **not** have an ambiguous case, because cosine gives a unique angle between 0 and 180 degrees. That is why the cosine rule is safer when finding angles.
If you are asked to 'show that' there are two possible values, find both and check each leaves a positive third angle.
core.h: The ambiguous case (SSA) - a Higher tier extension
core.p: When you are given two sides and an angle that is **not** between them (SSA), there can be two different triangles that fit the information. This is because the equation sin B = k has two solutions between 0 and 180 degrees: B and 180 − B. Whether both are possible depends on whether the second option leaves enough angle for the third angle to be positive. The diagram in this note shows a fixed angle at A, a fixed side AC, and a side BC that can 'swing' to meet the base line at two different points. Exam questions at GCSE usually state or imply which triangle is meant, but you should know that the second solution exists.

bullets: The formula can be written for any labelling: b² = a² + c² − 2ac cos B and c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
The pattern: (side opposite the angle)² = (other side)² + (other side)² − 2 × (other side) × (other side) × cos(the angle).
The angle used in cos is **between** the two sides that are multiplied.
If the angle is obtuse, cos is negative, so the 'minus 2bc cos A' term becomes a positive number added on.
Use the cosine rule when you know **two sides and the included angle (SAS)** or **all three sides (SSS)**.
The cosine rule is the one to choose whenever there is no side-opposite-angle pair to start the sine rule.
The rule is symmetrical in b and c, so it does not matter which order you use them in.
core.h: The cosine rule: statement and origin
core.p: The cosine rule is a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. It is Pythagoras' theorem with a correction term. When A = 90 degrees, cos A = 0 and the rule becomes a² = b² + c². When A is acute the correction **reduces** a² so the side is shorter than the hypotenuse of the equivalent right-angled triangle, and when A is obtuse cos A is negative so −2bc cos A is **added**, making the side longer. The rule comes from splitting the triangle into two right-angled triangles with a perpendicular height and applying Pythagoras to each. The rule always links **three sides and one angle**: the angle A is the one **opposite** side a, and it is the angle included between b and c.

bullets: Step 1: identify the two known sides and the included angle; call the unknown side a and its opposite angle A.
Step 2: write a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A with numbers substituted.
Step 3: work out the right-hand side; for sides 8 and 11 with included angle 52, a² = 64 + 121 − 2 × 8 × 11 × cos 52 = 185 − 108.35... = 76.64...
Step 4: square-root: a = 8.75 (3 s.f.).
Check: the answer must be less than the sum of the other two sides (8 + 11 = 19) and greater than their difference (3); this is the triangle inequality.
Do **not** square-root before subtracting: a is not b + c − 2bc cos A.
If the included angle is obtuse, expect cos to be negative, and watch the double negative in −2bc × (negative).
core.h: Using the cosine rule to find a side
core.p: With two sides and the included angle, substitute directly into a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, calculate the right-hand side, and then take the square root. The common error is to evaluate (b² + c² − 2bc) first and then multiply by cos A, which breaks the order of operations. Follow BIDMAS strictly: calculate b², c² and 2bc cos A separately, subtract the product from the sum of squares, then square-root. A calculator with natural display lets you type the expression in a single line, but writing the intermediate value (for example a² = 123.4) protects your method marks.

bullets: Formula: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc), where a is the side opposite the wanted angle A.
Example: sides 7, 9, 12 and the largest angle is opposite 12: cos θ = (7² + 9² − 12²) / (2 × 7 × 9) = (49 + 81 − 144) / 126 = −14 / 126 = −0.111..., so θ = 96.4 degrees.
A negative result for cos means the angle is **obtuse**; the calculator handles this automatically.
Put brackets round the entire numerator and denominator on a calculator, or work out each separately.
If the fraction is bigger than 1 or smaller than −1, the three sides cannot form a triangle.
After finding one angle, you can find a second angle with the sine rule or by repeating the cosine rule, then the third by subtraction from 180.
Check that the angles add up to 180 degrees and that the largest angle faces the longest side.
core.h: Using the cosine rule to find an angle
core.p: When all three sides are known, rearrange the cosine rule to make cos A the subject: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc). Put the side opposite the angle you want in the numerator with a minus sign, and use the other two sides in the rest of the formula. Then use inverse cosine (cos⁻¹). Because cosine is unique between 0 and 180 degrees, the calculator gives the correct angle even when it is obtuse, and a negative value for cos A tells you the angle is obtuse. Find the **largest** angle first (opposite the longest side), because then the other two must be acute and you can safely use the sine rule if you want.

bullets: The angle must be the one **between** the two sides used; this is the commonest mistake.
Example: sides 9 cm and 12 cm with included angle 38 degrees: area = ½ × 9 × 12 × sin 38 = 33.2 cm² (3 s.f.).
Reverse example: area 30 cm², sides 8 and 11: sin C = 2 × 30 / (8 × 11) = 60 / 88, so C = 43.0 degrees (or 137.0 degrees if the angle is obtuse).
Units of area are squared (cm², m²), and angles are in degrees.
For an equilateral triangle of side 6: area = ½ × 6 × 6 × sin 60 = 15.6 cm² (or exactly 9√3).
For exact-value questions, use sin 30 = ½, sin 45 = √2/2, sin 60 = √3/2 in the formula.
Area of a **sector minus triangle** gives the area of a segment in circle questions: segment = ½r²θ (in degrees: θ/360 × πr²) minus ½r² sin θ.
A parallelogram with sides a and b and angle C has area ab sin C (two triangles).
core.h: Area of a triangle: ½ab sin C
core.p: If you know two sides of a triangle and the angle **between** them, the area is ½ × a × b × sin C. This comes from the usual formula area = ½ × base × height, because if the base is a, the perpendicular height is h = b sin C, giving ½ × a × b sin C. It means you can find the area without knowing the perpendicular height. The same formula can be rearranged to find a missing side or angle when the area is given, and you can use it on any pair of sides with their included angle: ½bc sin A, ½ac sin B and ½ab sin C all give the same area.

bullets: Bearings: the interior angle is found using the fact that bearings are measured clockwise from north and that co-interior angles between parallel north lines add to 180.
Draw a clear sketch, mark all known values, and state which rule you are using each time.
When a quadrilateral is given, split it into two triangles with a diagonal; find the diagonal by the cosine rule in one triangle and use it in the other.
Keep unrounded values from step to step (use the ANS or memory function) and only round at the end, because rounding early can change the third significant figure.
For the area of a field or plot split into triangles, find each area with ½ab sin C and add.
3D problems on a face or cross-section often reduce to a flat triangle where these rules apply (see 3D trigonometry).
Explain in words if asked: 'Use the cosine rule because I know two sides and the included angle'.
Check the answer is realistic (a walk of 3 km should not come out as 300 km).
core.h: Putting it together: multi-step and applied problems
core.p: Many 5 or 6 mark questions need a chain of steps. A typical chain is: use the cosine rule for a side, then the sine rule for an angle, then ½ab sin C for the area, or the other way round. Another typical setting is **bearings**, where an angle in the triangle is found from the bearings given, then the rules are applied to find the distance between two ships or two walkers. Plan before you calculate: find any angle you can by simple rules first (angles in a triangle, angles on a straight line, alternate or co-interior angles).

bullets: Test your mode: sin 30 should display 0.5; if it shows −0.988, you are in radians.
Type cos⁻¹((7² + 9² − 12²) ÷ (2 × 7 × 9)) with brackets round the whole fraction.
Use the table of exact values for non-calculator parts: sin 30 = ½, cos 60 = ½, sin 60 = √3/2, cos 30 = √3/2, sin 45 = cos 45 = √2/2.
If the question says 'give your answer correct to 1 decimal place', do not give 3 significant figures.
Show the unrounded value (for example 8.7546...) before the rounded one to protect marks.
Higher tier link: the **area of a segment** needs both sector area and triangle area ½r² sin θ.
Higher tier link: **proof** questions may ask you to prove the area formula or show the sine rule from a diagram.
core.h: Accuracy, calculator technique and links to other topics
core.p: Accurate calculator use is worth many marks in this topic. Make sure the calculator is in **DEG** mode, use brackets when typing fractions, and use the stored answer rather than a rounded copy. Inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹) are accessed with SHIFT. Round only at the end, and give the answer to the accuracy asked, normally 3 significant figures for lengths and 1 decimal place for angles. This topic links to Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA (special cases), bearings, 3D problems, circle theorems (the circumcircle), vectors (the angle between two vectors) and arcs and sectors.

exam: **Command words**: 'Calculate' and 'Work out' need working shown; 'Show that' needs full working to the given value plus one more decimal; 'Find' means any valid method.
**1-2 mark** questions: a single application of one rule. Mark scheme: M1 for the correct substitution, A1 for the answer.
**3 mark** questions: usually find an angle first (angles sum to 180) then the sine rule. M1 third angle, M1 substitution, A1 answer.
**4-5 mark** questions combine two rules; each rule use is typically M1 A1. Write down the formula before substituting.

**6 mark** problem-solving (bearings, quadrilaterals, fields): plan with a labelled sketch; state each triangle you work in; accuracy marks depend on correct earlier answers (follow-through is allowed).
Always write the formula in its general form before substituting; this secures the method mark.
Show the unrounded answer, then the rounded one, e.g. 8.7546... = 8.75 cm.
Use the phrase 'cosine rule' or 'sine rule' in your working if the question asks you to **justify**.
For 'Prove' or 'Show' area questions, start from area = ½ × base × height and use sin C = h / b.
Check **the answer is sensible**: biggest angle opposite the longest side; angles add to 180.
Check the question asks for **area** or **length** or **angle** and the unit you give matches (cm, cm², °).

mistakes.r: Use the cosine rule for SAS and SSS; the sine rule needs a complete matching pair.
mistakes.w: Using the sine rule when there is no side-and-opposite-angle pair (e.g. SAS)

mistakes.r: Work out 2bc cos A as a product first, then subtract it from b² + c², then square-root.
mistakes.w: Calculating (b² + c² − 2bc) × cos A in the wrong order

mistakes.r: Find a² first, then square-root only as the very last step.
mistakes.w: Taking the square root too early, e.g. a = b + c − ...

mistakes.r: The angle must be the included angle between the two sides used.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong angle in ½ab sin C (an angle not between the two sides)

mistakes.r: Check DEG mode before starting; sin 30 must display 0.5.
mistakes.w: Calculator in radian mode, giving sin 30 = −0.988

mistakes.r: Keep full calculator values or use ANS; round only the final answer.
mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate values (e.g. sin 65 as 0.91) and losing accuracy

mistakes.r: Put the unknown on top; use a/sinA for sides and sinA/a for angles.
mistakes.w: Writing the sine rule upside down so the unknown is on the bottom, then forgetting to flip

mistakes.r: If the angle is obtuse, the answer is 180 minus the calculator value (sine rule); the cosine rule gives it directly.
mistakes.w: Giving an acute angle when the diagram shows an obtuse one

mistakes.r: Lengths in cm, areas in cm², angles in degrees (°).
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or writing cm instead of cm² for area

summary: You must be able to find missing sides and angles in any triangle using the sine rule and the cosine rule, choosing the correct rule from the information given, and calculate the area of a triangle using ½ab sin C. These rules extend right-angled trigonometry to every triangle and appear in multi-step problems on bearings, 3D shapes and circle geometry.

terms.d: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C; relates sides to the sines of their opposite angles in any triangle.
a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A; relates three sides and one angle in any triangle.
The side of a triangle that does not touch a given angle; it is labelled with the matching lower-case letter.
The angle between two given sides.
Side-angle-side: two sides and the included angle are known; use the cosine rule to find the third side.
Three sides are known; use the cosine rule to find an angle.
Two angles and a side are known; find the third angle (angles sum to 180) then use the sine rule.
Two sides and a non-included angle; may give two possible triangles.
sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹: the calculator functions that return an angle from a ratio.
½ab sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b.
The shortest distance from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension); h = b sin C.
An angle greater than 90 degrees and less than 180 degrees; its cosine is negative.
Any side of a triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two sides.
The circle passing through all three vertices; its diameter equals a / sin A.
The calculator setting in which angles are measured in degrees; essential for these formulae.

worked.q: In triangle ABC, angle A = 48°, angle B = 65° and BC = a = 7.2 cm. Calculate the length of AC (side b). (3 marks)
